bp: Personal data question answering starts from a familiar frustration: a person's life is recorded in many small systems, but the useful answer often lives across all of them. A calendar knows meetings, a workout log knows exercise, purchase records know spending, mail knows arrangements, and social posts know public activity. A user does not usually want one record back. They ask analytic questions such as how often something happened, what changed over a period, or which events satisfy a time condition. PerQA serves the researchers and builders who need to test whether question-answering systems can do that kind of work over heterogeneous personal data. The paper is not primarily proposing a new assistant. It builds a benchmark from synthetic personas, then asks realistic questions over those personas. The need comes before the method: without a shared test, systems can look good on ordinary text questions while still failing at the everyday task of reasoning over a person's scattered, time-stamped life traces.
wh: The difficulty is that personal information is not one clean document. It is many kinds of evidence, each with its own shape. Calendar entries have dates, times, and titles. Purchases have merchants, prices, and maybe categories. Workouts have durations and activity types. Mail and social media are more open-ended text. A question may cut across several of these sources and may include a temporal condition, so the system must first understand what period matters, then find all matching events, then aggregate them correctly. A simple reading system can answer a fact written in one paragraph, but PerQA-style questions often require counting, filtering, comparing, and joining records that were never written as one story. The benchmark itself is also hard to construct. It must avoid exposing real private lives, so it uses synthetic personas, yet the resulting questions still need to feel like questions real people would ask. The local-student user study checks that realism pressure.
naive: A smart beginner would collect all personal records, turn them into text, and ask a language model to answer the user's question directly. That can work for a question whose answer appears plainly in one message or one calendar entry. It breaks when the answer is distributed. For example, a question about workouts during a certain month requires finding every relevant workout, excluding records outside the time window, and adding or comparing them. A second naive approach would build one hand-written rule per source type. That fails because personal questions vary too much: some ask about purchases, some about mail, some combine sources, and many express time indirectly. PerQA exists because these simple tests do not reveal whether a system can handle the full scattered record.
ap: The core move is to make the hidden task visible as a benchmark. PerQA constructs synthetic people with multiple kinds of personal data, then generates questions through repeated prompting of language models, followed by checks that the questions are realistic information needs. This design creates a controlled world where the answer is knowable, but the work still resembles the messy real task: the system must move between structured records and text, respect time, and often compute an aggregate over many events. The benchmark therefore tests more than fluent answering. It tests whether a method can retrieve the right pieces of a person's history, interpret the temporal wording in the question, combine evidence from heterogeneous sources, and return an answer that reflects all relevant records rather than the easiest record to mention. The experiments with a suite of methods then measure both current difficulty and the room for smarter designs.
mech: The mechanism begins by creating synthetic personas, which are fictional but coherent people whose personal histories can contain calendar entries, workouts, purchases, mail, social media, and other records. This matters because the benchmark needs private-life complexity without using real private data. For each persona, the data forms a small personal universe: different sources describe different slices of the same person's activity. The next step is question generation. The paper uses iterative language-model prompting, meaning prompts are refined over rounds so the questions are not just simple lookups. Many questions are analytic: they ask the system to count, aggregate, compare, or filter many events. A large fraction also includes temporal conditions, so the answer depends on dates, ranges, ordering, or time-sensitive phrasing. After question construction, a user study with local students asks whether these generated questions match realistic information needs. That is a quality check on the benchmark, not just on the answering systems. Finally, multiple question-answering methods are run on PerQA. Each method receives a question and the relevant personal-data environment, then must produce an answer. The benchmark scores whether the method can find the right evidence, transform records into the needed comparison or aggregate, and avoid answering from a single tempting fragment when the question actually requires many fragments.
math: The central mathematical idea is not an exotic formula; it is disciplined bookkeeping under uncertainty. Aggregation means turning many records into one answer by counting, summing, grouping, or comparing them. The hard part is deciding which records belong in the pile before doing the arithmetic. Temporal reasoning adds an ordering structure: every event sits on a timeline, and the question defines a window or relation on that timeline. The system must translate words such as during, before, after, recent, or between into inclusion rules. Retrieval and ranking also appear. When a question is asked, there may be many possible records, so the system needs a way to bring the useful few forward before answering. Ranking is just sorting candidates by expected usefulness, but here usefulness depends on source type, content, and time. Probability enters because the system is often unsure which records match the user's wording, especially for mail or social text. The benchmark asks whether methods can manage the tradeoff between completeness and noise: include too few records and the aggregate is wrong; include too many and unrelated events pollute the answer. PerQA is mathematical because it turns a personal-history question into selection, time filtering, evidence combination, and answer checking.
dots: In the repo's current theme data, PerQA sits near LLMs and language models, social or personal data, information retrieval, ranking, and probability. That placement is natural. Like retrieval-augmented question answering papers, it asks whether an answering system can ground its response in external evidence rather than fluent guesswork. Like ranking papers, it faces the problem of choosing a small working set from a large pile of possible records. Like probability-centered papers, it must keep uncertainty visible when evidence is partial, repeated, delayed, or scattered. It also connects to privacy and personalization work, although the abstract only supports the benchmark side directly: personal data is useful precisely because it is intimate and specific, which makes real-data evaluation sensitive. PerQA's neighboring idea is that future assistants will not only answer public web facts. They will answer questions over calendars, receipts, messages, and activity traces, where time and aggregation are first-class parts of the problem.
ww: PerQA works as an evaluation idea because it forces the system to face the shape of the real problem rather than a simplified substitute. Ordinary question-answering tests often reward finding one passage that states the answer. Personal analytic questions punish that shortcut. If the question asks how many relevant events occurred in a period, the system must collect all matching events, not just the most obvious one. If the data spans calendars, purchases, workouts, mail, and social media, the system must understand that the same person's life is represented in several incompatible formats. Synthetic personas make the test repeatable and safer than using real private data, while the student study checks that the generated questions are not just artificial puzzles. The iterative prompting used to create questions should help widen the benchmark beyond template-like lookups. The experiments then reveal a useful gap: existing methods struggle, but smart designs make progress, which means the benchmark is neither solved nor impossible.
po: The payoff is a shared testbed for a class of assistants that people are likely to want: systems that can answer questions about their own scattered records. PerQA gives researchers synthetic personas, heterogeneous personal data, and temporally sensitive analytic questions, then shows through experiments that current question-answering methods find the task difficult. The local-student user study adds evidence that the questions resemble real information needs. Practically, this lets future systems be judged on whether they can filter by time, aggregate over events, and work across many personal data types instead of only answering questions over clean public text.
limits: The main assumption is that synthetic personas are close enough to real personal histories to teach useful lessons. The user study supports realism of the questions, but the abstract does not prove that the synthetic data captures the full messiness, incompleteness, privacy sensitivity, or emotional stakes of real personal records. The questions are generated by iterative language-model prompting, so they may inherit the generator's habits. The abstract also does not specify which answering methods were tested, what error types dominated, or whether success transfers to deployed assistants with live, changing data. PerQA establishes a benchmark and a difficulty signal, not a complete solution.
